newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Unknown Russian shares seen hottest in slow summer.
newsitem.headline: Unknown Russian shares seen hottest in slow summer.

text.p: Shares in Russia's regional power companies may surge over the next month, but the country's leading shares will be mixed as major investors await U.S. interest rate and Russian budget news, analysts said on Tuesday.

Established Western investors are retrenching from leading shares to lesser-known ones over the medium term as a trickle of new capital comes in, supporting but not significantly moving the most liquid names in the market.
"Power generation is the most interesting and attractive sector and it will remain that," said a Western analyst at a Moscow brokerage.

He said regional power utilities sparked by reform at national electric company Unified Energy System (UES), which has 49 percent or larger stakes in 70 of Russia's 72 regional utilities, would outperform the market in the short term.
"UES will remain at the centre of attention, but there is going to be more focus on second and third line companies."
Eldon Capital Management Emerging Markets investment chief Phillip Manduca said investors would reallocate funds.
"The theme of the next six months will be diversification out of the top six or seven stocks," he told an investor conference.

Troika Dialog Asset Management chief Nancy Herring said leading shares would climb slightly over the next month or two and the Russian Trading System (RTS) 22-share index would climb to test new highs.
But the index, which closed at 355.35 on Tuesday after 355.46 on Monday, does not have far to go to match its record 366.80 set on May 19, the end of a dip since mid-February.

Herring said new foreign funds over the next couple of months would increase foreign equity investment for the year to date by 25 percent and total investment through the end of the year would be about 50 percent more than now.
She declined to give absolute numbers but said foreign funds would outweigh local investment despite increased interest.
Share analysts and traders are divided on the extent to which U.S. interest rate policy is holding back foreign investment.
But some say investors are waiting for the Federal Reserve, which has raised rates once this year, to make its intentions clear.
"The short-term is driven by what is happening in the U.S.," said the Moscow analyst. "Longer term there are a lot of good things happening in Russia."

But large funds are seen holding back from injecting new waves of capital, despite good reform news, by worries over the Russian budget and a tax code which investors hope will bring new clarity to the market but may not pass parliament this year.
Government forecasts made public on Tuesday put 1997 gross domestic product at flat to down two percent on 1996. Early this year officials had predicted two percent growth.

United City Bank research chief Christopher Granville told the Euromoney conference that Westerners were focused on the tax code. "It is a key issue that many investors rightly think of as a litmus test for reforms," he said.
